title: The BERA scandal dwarfs the Arday case
author: Vainker, Stephen
summary: Stephen Vainker argues that the British Educational Research Association has presided over a systematic failure of peer review by publishing AI-written academic articles submitted by authors from countries with weaker academic integrity enforcement — a direct and foreseeable consequence of BERA's Race Equity Policy targeting diversity in authorship over quality. He documents how BERA's commitment to 'no detriment on quality' while diversifying authorship was never credible, presents examples of obviously low-quality articles that could not have passed meaningful peer review, and shows how BERA responded to his findings with denial and limited retraction rather than systematic remediation. The article situates BERA alongside the Jason Arday case as evidence of a broader institutional failure: educational academia has prioritised identity markers in hiring and publication over the quality of knowledge produced. Vainker argues that BERA's response — labelling his methodology ethically problematic — reflects an institution protecting its reputation rather than its scholarly mission.
points: BERA has published somewhere between dozens and hundreds of articles written by AI, submitted by authors from countries without robust academic integrity enforcement.

BERA aims to increase the range and diversity of authors being published in the journals and is reliant on Wiley, adding 'there will be no detriment on quality.' It is remarkable how cavalier BERA are about the potential trade-off.
The articles are so bad that it is clear that peer review cannot have occurred in any meaningful sense — I have numerous examples across the four BERA journals demonstrating this.
BERA labelled my approach 'ethically problematic' and has only taken action in a small number of cases where it falsely claimed to have independently uncovered the evidence.

The Arday story matters because it shows a university placing its own interests — demonstrating its commitment to EDI — above its core purpose: to produce knowledge that is significant and can be trusted.
quotes: However, the basis for their retraction was misleading and self-serving in two ways: They suggested that in investigating my claims, they ‘uncovered independently that the peer review process for a limited number of articles in the British Educational Research Journal (BERJ) had been manipulated’.

BERA - another institution failing in its core purpose In conclusion, here are the three ways in which BERA have allowed EDI targets to completely distort their core role: Refuse to foresee any potential conflict between increasing author diversity and retaining quality.

Academic leaders are totally invested in targets that legitimate themselves, such as EDI objectives, but they are completely lacking in the perspicacity to implement these objectives in ways that enhance, and do not detract from the core academic mission.

The phrase ‘uncovered independently’ is ridiculous, since before they began their investigation I had already provided evidence that an editor of the special section was engaged in highly suspicious peer review practices.

But somehow the leaders at the British Educational Research Association are more invested in retaining their shaky legitimacy by denying the possibility of any issue than ensuring that the work they publish has integrity.

They further write that ‘retraction notices should be published as soon as the editor is confident that the publication is seriously flawed, misleading, or falls into any of the categories described above’.
My own approach (which BERA labelled ‘ethically problematic’) is to find phrases that, according to Google Scholar, were not in use, or barely in use, before 2023 but have become (more) common since.
